extracts.author: Guglielmo Gratarolo
extracts.essence: A doctor's guide to keeping a healthy memory, which ends with a complete step-by-step method for building one from places and images.
points: Written in Latin by an Italian physician in 1553, then translated into English in 1562 by a London merchant, William Fulwood, who dedicated it to Queen Elizabeth's favourite, Robert Dudley.
Memory is treated as part of the body. It lives at the back of the brain, and too much cold and damp spoils it.
The cures are homely: rub your limbs, avoid garlic and late-night drinks, wash your feet in herb-scented water.
The last chapter is the art itself. Choose a large, familiar house, mark every fifth place with a sign so you can count, and fill the places with people you know doing something odd.

Five rules for images: move the feelings; use likeness or opposites; start young and practise daily; repeat each group of five; join simple images into compound ones. A chickpea (cicer) in a garden (hortus) can stand for Cicero against Hortensius.
extracts.picture: A friend you know well pours a pot of water over another friend's head. Two names, one unforgettable scene.
extracts.tryit: Pick five new words you want to keep. Put each in a different room of a house you know, with a person from your life doing something ridiculous with it.

extracts.short: The Jewel House of Art and Nature
extracts.author: Hugh Plat
extracts.essence: An inventor passes on a fast room-by-room method, then admits it falls short of the hype.
points: Plat was a restless collector of useful tricks, from fuel balls to recipes. His memory chapter passes on the system taught in London by Alexander Dickson, a follower of Giordano Bruno.
Choose a big building and fix ten 'subjects' in each room: a soldier at the door, a burning fire at the bed's head, a dunghill at its foot, an ape on the cupboard, a ship in the window.
To remember a list, make each word do something violent or silly to the subject in its place. A cat scratches the soldier until he bleeds. A lute burns in the fire.
Plat found it good for ten to forty things and used it for errands and anecdotes. But he mocks Dickson's high fees and big promises, and he notes that some pupils used it to cheat at cards.
extracts.picture: A cat clawing a soldier's face at the door, a lute cracking in the fireplace, a hand raking the dunghill at the foot of the bed.
extracts.tryit: Fix ten 'subjects' in one room of your home, in order. Ask a friend for three words and place them in the first three.
extracts.search: Jewel House of Art and Nature Hugh Plat 1594

extracts.short: A Help to Memory and Discourse
extracts.author: William Basse
extracts.essence: A question-and-answer jest-book shows the memory art arriving in popular print, praised and kept at arm's length.
points: A companion to a 1619 miscellany of jokes, riddles and wise sayings, made for young gentlemen who wanted to shine in conversation.
Good talk needs a good memory. Memory is frail, and it is compared to the Tower of London, where the realm's records were kept.

The writer reports what the memory-art authors say: places are like paper and images like letters. He supports it with Bible examples: twelve stones in the Jordan, sacraments as visible signs, a thread tied round a finger.
He does not practise it himself. He leaves the art to the specialists and trusts a natural memory strengthened by God, though he does not look down on other help.
extracts.picture: Memory as a clerk keeping records in a great stone tower, with some entries carved deep and others wiped out like chalk.
extracts.tryit: Where would you keep your most important memories if you had to store them in a building? Describe the building and the rooms.
extracts.search: Help to Memory and Discourse Basse 1620

extracts.author: John Willis
extracts.essence: The fullest English handbook: a complete memory theatre, built like a real building, with rules for size, position, colour and sound.
points: Willis, a shorthand inventor, says writing is the best memory aid, and that the art of places and images is closest to writing. Places are the pages, images the letters.
Proof by stories: Simonides identifies the crushed guests at a banquet by where each sat, and Darius wins a kingdom because his horse neighs at the right place.
Seeing beats hearing. So picture the thing as if you were looking at it, the way a doctor remembers an anatomy lesson.
The 'repository' is a stone theatre with a stage and a central pillar, drawn to exact measurements. Each repository has its own pillar colour, and every image placed in it wears that colour.
Images take their natural position (pictures on walls, books on shelves, graves under the stage), their natural sound and smell, and they are enlarged or shrunk to fit.
Also keep a pocket notebook of striking sentences, sorted under headings.
extracts.picture: A man steps outside a banquet hall just before the roof falls in. Afterwards he can name every crushed guest, because he remembers where each one sat.
extracts.tryit: Pick one real event from last week. Walk through the rooms where it happened and say what you saw in each one.

extracts.short: The Art of Memory Made Plain
extracts.author: Henry Herdson
extracts.essence: A self-styled Cambridge professor sells the art to ordinary people: shopkeepers, sermon-goers and Bible readers.
points: Almost nothing is known about Herdson, apart from a rumour that he advertised himself as a 'Professor of the Art of Memory' and a famous scholar did not remember ever meeting him.
His palace has four chambers, 21 tables and 105 imagined friends, each holding images for numbers.
Practical uses: a shopkeeper pictures an acquaintance in a cloak of cloth and holds the number of yards in one hand and the price in the other.
Sermons are divided into parts, each placed in the repository. Bible stories are split into people: Genesis becomes Adam, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Joseph.
For scripture, give each book of the Bible a friend with a similar name. Use the right hand for the chapter and the left for the verse.
Two ways to fix an image: surround it with the most delightful things for all five senses ('paradise'), or the most disgusting ('hell').
extracts.picture: A friend named John, standing in the library of your mind, who stands for the Gospel of John. Chapter in his right hand, verse in his left.
extracts.tryit: Take a story you know well and split it into five people. Put each in a different corner of a room.
extracts.search: Herdson Ars Memoriae Art of Memory Made Plain 1651

extracts.author: Richard Saunders
extracts.essence: The hand as a memory machine: ten letters on the palm, and Ramon Llull's turning wheels of ideas.
points: Saunders, an almanac writer and physician, tucked this into a book about palm-reading and character-reading, translated from the French writer Jean Belot.
Llull, a medieval thinker, built a system of turning wheels that could combine ideas in every possible way. Saunders makes it practical by writing the letters on your hand.
The letters B to K run round the base of the thumb and fingers, with A in the middle of the palm.
Each letter is a question: who? of what? why? how much? what kind? when? where? how? Together they can organise almost any subject.
The method is promised to make even a seven-year-old good in the sciences within ten days. Preachers can map Bible stories onto the letters, and merchants can map their business.
extracts.picture: Your own open hand, with a letter on the palm and a letter at the root of each finger, and a question hanging from each.
extracts.tryit: Take a problem you have. Put one question on each finger and the palm, and answer them in turn.
extracts.search: Saunders Physiognomie and Chiromancie Art of Memory 1671

extracts.author: Marius D'Assigny
extracts.essence: A late, clear summary of everything earlier in Part I, with a cautious word about its limits.
points: D'Assigny was a teacher and translator who wrote for 'the young students of both universities'. He pulls together the best of earlier writers without naming all of them.
Some use a building with coloured pillars. Others put beasts on the letters of the alphabet, and parts of the body as places, to get 115 places.
A better option is to use your own town, with its gates, streets and churches, or a big empty house with rooms numbered by distance from the door.
Make images remarkable, ridiculous or moving. Represent a person by likeness or contrast: Galen by another doctor, Ovid by a big nose, Plato by broad shoulders.
He admits the method is awkward and not suited to everyone, and not meant for speeches. It is best for names, dates and notable passages.
Eight rules, including: reread the material first, give images action, stir the feelings, never reuse an image, and recall them in order. Do it last thing at night, when the mind is quiet.
extracts.picture: You enter your home town by the gate and walk its streets in order, each church and friend's house holding one thing you want to keep.
extracts.tryit: Tonight, before sleep, list five things you want to remember tomorrow. Walk through five places and put one in each.
